concepts.name: Population Density: Patterns, Anomalies and Determinants
key_dimensions: Distinction between arithmetic density, physiological density and agricultural density — UPSC often tests which metric is used in Census
States with counterintuitive density values (e.g., Arunachal Pradesh lowest ~17/km², Bihar highest among large states ~1,106/km²)
Role of physiographic vs. socio-economic factors in determining density (river plains vs. plateaus vs. mountains)
Comparison of India's overall density (382/km² in 2011) with global and regional benchmarks

concepts.name: Census 2011: Key Demographic Indicators and Their Geographical Interpretation
key_dimensions: Total population (1.21 billion), decadal growth rate (17.7%) and its decline from 21.5% in 2001 — significance of slowdown
State-wise population share anomalies: UP (16.5%) vs. Sikkim (0.05%) — implications for delimitation and resource allocation
Difference between population growth rate and natural growth rate (birth rate minus death rate) — trap question
Provisional vs. final Census data reliability and use of Sample Registration System (SRS) in intercensal periods

concepts.name: Physiographic Determinism in Population Distribution: Plains, Plateaus and Mountains
key_dimensions: Indo-Gangetic Plain: why it holds ~40% of India's population despite being ~25% of land area — alluvial fertility, irrigation, connectivity
Deccan Plateau: moderate density — role of rain-shadow effect, hard rock aquifers limiting agriculture
Himalayan and North-Eastern regions: sparse population — terrain, climate, insurgency, connectivity barriers
Coastal plains (Konkan vs. Coromandel vs. Malabar) — differential density driven by historical trade, fisheries and urbanisation

concepts.name: Sex Ratio: Overall, Child and State-level Variations
key_dimensions: Overall sex ratio (940 in 2011 vs. 933 in 2001) — improving trend but still below 1,000; Kerala (1,084) vs. Haryana (879) extremes
Child Sex Ratio (0–6 years): 914 in 2011 — declined from 927 in 2001 despite overall sex ratio improvement (the key UPSC trap)
Why states with high literacy/income (Punjab, Haryana, Delhi) have low child sex ratio — 'son meta-preference' paradox
Union territories anomaly: Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli have low sex ratio due to male migrant workers — not reflective of social bias

concepts.name: Literacy Rate: Spatial Disparities and Composite Determinants
key_dimensions: National literacy rate (74.04% in 2011) — definition trap: persons aged 7 years and above who can read and write
Gender literacy gap: Male 82.14% vs. Female 65.46% — states where gap is narrowing (Kerala, Mizoram) vs. widening
Rajasthan's female literacy (52.66%) as lowest among major states vs. Bihar's overall literacy (63.82%) — different metrics, common confusion
Relationship between literacy, fertility rate and population growth — demographic transition linkage

concepts.name: Population Growth Trajectory: Stages of Demographic Transition in India
key_dimensions: Four phases of population growth in India (stagnant pre-1921, slow 1921–1951, rapid 1951–1981, decelerating post-1981)
1921 as the 'Year of the Great Divide' — why it is a demographic watershed
Differential stage of demographic transition across states: Kerala near Stage 4, UP/Bihar in Stage 2-3 — policy implications
Replacement level fertility (TFR of 2.1) — states that have achieved it vs. those that haven't, and UPSC trap of equating TFR decline with population decline

concepts.name: Migration: Types, Patterns and Impact on Population Distribution
key_dimensions: Rural-to-urban vs. rural-to-rural migration streams — Census data shows rural-to-rural is numerically dominant (often surprises candidates)
Inter-state migration hotspots: UP and Bihar as major source states; Maharashtra, Delhi, Gujarat as destination states
Reasons for migration: economic (work/employment largest stream for males), marriage (largest stream for females — UPSC trap)
Impact of migration on source regions (remittances, demographic hollowing) and destination regions (urban primacy, slum growth)

concepts.name: Scheduled Tribe (ST) Population Distribution: Geographical Concentration and Anomalies
key_dimensions: ST population is 8.6% of total (2011) but spatially concentrated in Central India (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, MP) and NE India
Mizoram, Meghalaya, Nagaland have >80% ST population — not classified as 'Tribal Belt' in conventional sense — conceptual trap
Fifth Schedule vs. Sixth Schedule areas: geographical distribution and which states fall under which schedule
Paradox: states with large absolute ST numbers (MP, Odisha) vs. states with high ST percentage (Mizoram, Lakshadweep)

concepts.name: Population Distribution and the North–South Demographic Divide
key_dimensions: BIMARU states (Bihar, MP, Rajasthan, UP) have high TFR, low HDI and contribute disproportionately to national population growth
Southern states (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh) near replacement TFR — likely to see population share decline post-delimitation
Delimitation controversy: freezing of seats based on 1971 Census and implications of using 2011 or future Census data
North–South divide in age structure: southern states ageing faster — different demand for social infrastructure (pensions vs. schools)

concepts.name: Urban Population Distribution: Classification and Criteria for Urban Areas
key_dimensions: Census definition of urban area: (a) statutory towns, (b) census towns — criteria: 5,000+ population, 75%+ male non-agricultural workers, density 400/km²
Difference between 'statutory town', 'census town', 'outgrowth' and 'urban agglomeration' — frequently tested definitional trap
Sharp rise in census towns from 1,362 (2001) to 3,894 (2011) — what it reveals about peri-urban growth without governance upgradation
Urban population share (31.16% in 2011) — India still below world average (~55%) — implications for urbanisation trajectory

concepts.name: Mega-Cities and Urban Agglomerations: Primacy and Spatial Distribution
key_dimensions: Four million-plus urban agglomerations (UAs) with 10M+ population: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai — their regional dominance
Urban primacy: Delhi UA surpassing Mumbai UA in 2011 — reasons (capital city effect, migration, NCR expansion)
Difference between 'city proper', 'urban agglomeration' and 'metropolitan area' — Census vs. administrative definitions
Secondary cities (Tier-2) growing faster than mega-cities post-2001 — significance for balanced regional development

concepts.name: Rural Population Distribution: Characteristics and Regional Patterns
key_dimensions: India still 68.84% rural (2011) — but states like Goa (37.8% rural) and Delhi (2.5% rural) are anomalies to national trend
Relationship between village size and region: large nucleated villages in the Gangetic Plain vs. small dispersed hamlets in hilly/tribal areas
Declining share of rural population in successive Censuses — but absolute rural numbers still increasing (rural population rose by 90 million 2001–2011)
Rural-urban continuum: reclassification of villages as census towns — impact on rural development schemes targeting rural population

concepts.name: Age Structure and Dependency Ratio: Demographic Dividend and Its Geography
key_dimensions: India's median age (~28 years) and the window of demographic dividend (2020–2040) — uneven across states
Difference between age dependency ratio, child dependency ratio and old-age dependency ratio — which is relevant for demographic dividend calculation
States already past demographic dividend window (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) vs. states yet to enter it (UP, Bihar) — policy divergence
Youth bulge in BIMARU states as either dividend or disaster depending on skill development and employment generation

concepts.name: Population and Natural Resource Correlation: Carrying Capacity Concept
key_dimensions: Concept of carrying capacity and over-population vs. under-population — not purely about absolute numbers but resource–population ratio
Arunachal Pradesh: lowest density but also lowest carrying capacity utilisation — resource-rich but infrastructurally weak
West Bengal: high density (~1,029/km²) sustained by high agricultural productivity and industrial base — not necessarily over-populated
Groundwater depletion, land fragmentation and soil degradation as indicators of population pressure exceeding carrying capacity in NW India

concepts.name: Religious and Linguistic Population Distribution: Census Data and Controversies
key_dimensions: Muslim population concentration: UP, West Bengal, Assam, Kerala, J&K — but no single state has Muslim majority except J&K (pre-2019)
Differential growth rates across religious communities (Census 2001 and 2011) — convergence narrative vs. divergence perception
Linguistic distribution: Hindi belt dominance in northern population corridor vs. Dravidian language states in south — Eighth Schedule languages
States with high linguistic/religious minority concentration and their overlap with conflict zones, border areas — security dimension

concepts.name: Workers and Non-Workers: Workforce Participation Rate and Its Geography
key_dimensions: Worker Population Ratio (WPR) — India's WPR ~39.8% (2011); female WPR (25.5%) much lower than male (53.3%) — spatial variation
Main workers vs. marginal workers distinction — high proportion of marginal workers in tribal, rain-fed agricultural states indicates disguised unemployment
States with high female WPR: Himachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh — not the most 'developed' states — counters simple literacy-employment link
Cultivators declining, agricultural labourers increasing — shift within primary sector indicating land concentration and distress

concepts.name: Population Policy in India: National Population Policy 2000 and Target-Free Approach
key_dimensions: Shift from target-based (1952–1996) to target-free approach in National Population Policy 2000 — why the shift matters for spatial equity
NPP 2000 goals: immediate (unmet contraceptive need), medium-term (TFR 2.1 by 2010 — missed), long-term (stable population by 2045)
Coercive sterilisation history (Emergency 1975–77) and its geographic and demographic legacy in northern states — trust deficit in family planning
Two-child norm debates: states implementing incentive/disincentive policies and constitutional/ethical challenges — overlap with Article 21

concepts.name: Slum Population Distribution: Urban Poverty Geography
key_dimensions: Census 2011: 65.49 million slum dwellers in 4,041 towns — but 'notified', 'recognised' and 'identified' slums have different legal statuses (UPSC definitional trap)
Maharashtra has highest slum population (11.8 million) but Andhra Pradesh has highest share of urban population in slums (35.6%) — absolute vs. relative trap
Slums not exclusively a mega-city problem — Census 2011 shows significant slum population in smaller Class II and Class III towns
Correlation between slum growth and inadequacy of urban planning, rent control laws, and rural-urban migration streams

concepts.name: Decadal Growth Rate Variations Across States: Convergence or Divergence?
key_dimensions: Nagaland's negative growth rate in 2011 Census (−0.6%) — only state to record population decline — reasons: out-migration, boundary disputes affecting enumeration
Meghalaya's highest decadal growth rate (27.9%) among NE states — demographic vs. political implications
Convergence hypothesis: high-growth states slowing down (UP, Bihar growth fell) but absolute additions still enormous
Difference between declining growth rate and declining population — most UPSC distractors exploit this confusion

concepts.name: Population Distribution and Infrastructure: Railways, Roads and Electrification Nexus
key_dimensions: Positive feedback loop: high population density → justifies infrastructure investment → attracts further migration and economic activity
Sparse population in NE India and infrastructure deficit — chicken-and-egg problem for development planning
Road density (km of road per 100 km² of area) vs. per capita road availability — Kerala has high road density, low per capita because of high population
Electrification and its role in retaining population in rural areas vs. push-migration to cities — Saubhagya Scheme geographic targeting rationale
